extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of art, architecture, garden design, and aesthetic theory; general readers of philosophy of art
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for producing and evaluating works in fine art (painting, sculpture), architecture, and garden design, emphasizing perceptual effects, formal causes, and the role of the beholder's imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's aim — show life and the nature of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Every work of art really aims at showing us life and things as they are in truth; every genuine and successful work of art answers, for perception, the question 'What is life?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art presents a perceptible image that brings the nature of existence to the beholder; this is distinct from philosophy which seeks an explicit, permanent conceptual answer. Evaluate art by how well it gives a perceptual (not merely conceptual) insight into life. Anti-pattern: works that only restate a dry conception without perceptual richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave something for the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art must not give everything directly to the senses; it should present only what leads the fancy on the right path and leave the ultimate thing for the imagination to do ('something... must always be left over for the fancy to do').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms that invite the spectator's imaginative completion. Examples: sketches of great masters often effect more than their finished pictures because they leave space for imagination. Anti-pattern: wax figures — they give both form and colour so the imagination is left out and no aesthetic effect results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require co-operation of the beholder
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic effect depends upon the co‑operation of the beholder: a work must excite the fancy and cannot leave it inactive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work prompts active perceptual imagination in viewers rather than passive consumption. If viewers must 'address' the work (trying to force it to speak) they will only hear themselves; good work lets the work 'speak' and invites inward contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid communicating a mere distinct conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A work which proceeds from mere distinct conceptions is always ungenuine; if the author could state in words beforehand what he intends, the artistic medium was the wrong choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work arises from perceptual insight (idea perceived before being thought) rather than being an attempt to clothe a fully articulated concept in artistic form. Anti-pattern: art that could be replaced by an abstract statement without loss of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of inspired, immediate works vs. over‑deliberate works
rubrics_metrics.description: Works completed in the inspiration of the first conception (sketches, spontaneous melodies, lyrical songs) often have a more inevitable and delightful effect than large, deliberate works which mix inspiration with technical filling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging long, planned works (epics, grand operas, historical paintings), allow for inevitable admixture of less inspired, wearisome parts; judge spontaneous pieces for immediacy and unity of feeling. Examples: sketches often surpass finished pictures; long epics may contain 'insipid and wearisome' passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary playing with means (the bungler)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arbitrary playing with the means of art without a proper knowledge of the end is the fundamental characteristic of the dabbler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for aimlessness or decorative gestures that are not motivated by the work's end: pillars that support nothing, aimless volutes, meaningless musical runs, jingling rhymes. These indicate lack of understanding of the art's purpose and should be penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium should not supply everything (leave room for imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media appeal differently to imagination: sculpture gives form without colour, painting gives colour but only the appearance of form; giving both form and colour (as in wax figures) removes imaginative participation and destroys the aesthetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the chosen medium stimulates rather than quenches the viewer's imagination. Anti-pattern: hyper‑realistic reproductions that eliminate imaginative engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: English/Chinese garden principle — conceal art
rubrics_metrics.description: The English (or Chinese) garden principle: conceal art so that it appears as if nature had moved freely; an uncultivated, man‑absent spot decorates itself with tasteful, unforced grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge gardens by how well they give the impression that nature has been left free — tasteful grouping of plants, avoidance of overtly imposed geometrical forms. Anti-pattern: highly controlled, clipped, imposed shapes that reveal the owner's will rather than nature's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden design: objective vs subjective planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference between objective (English/Chinese) gardens planned in an objective spirit to express nature's will and French gardens planned subjectively to mirror the possessor's will (clipped hedges, trees cut into forms, straight alleys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor designs that manifest the will of nature (objective) rather than the will of the owner (subjective). When evaluating, penalize displays of domination over nature that prioritize forced forms or visible 'tokens of slavery'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture's fundamental theme — support and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The one constant theme of architecture is support and burden; its fundamental law is that no burden shall be without sufficient support, and no support without a suitable burden, with the relation exactly fitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate buildings by clarity and honesty in displaying structural relations: separation of support (columns) and burden (entablature) is ideal. Anti-patterns: elements that appear unsupported (e.g., suspended balconies) or supports without apparent burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of support and burden increases aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic effect appears when support and burden are separated (column and entablature); fused conditions (plain wall as both) lack effect. Intermediate devices (pilasters, vault+pillar) indicate degrees toward separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how clearly structural roles are expressed. The clearer the separation (colonnade vs plain wall), the stronger the perceived aesthetic effect. Use of painted indications when real separation is impractical is acceptable to suggest the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support must be ample but not excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: Support is not merely adapted when just sufficient; it should be so amply convenient that at first glance we feel at ease, yet superfluity of support must not exceed a degree that makes us perceive support without burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'line of equilibrium' and classical proportioning (entasis) to judge appropriate tapering and visible strength. Examples: columns with slight entasis; anti‑pattern: visibly over‑strong supports or supports that appear unnecessary (support without burden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form should be determined by structural end (function dictates form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form of architectural elements (e.g., the column) has its sole ground in affording the simplest and most suitable support; forms inconsistent with structural ends (twisted columns) are immediately judged shameless or in bad taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether stylistic choices are justified by structural needs. Penalize gratuitous ornamentation or shapes chosen for caprice rather than function (twisted columns, grouped columns where uniform distribution is required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and mass: architecture needs large masses for aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture as a fine art requires considerable size — only great masses make the action of gravitation apparent and impressive; ceteris paribus, the aesthetic effect increases with size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging buildings aesthetically, consider whether scale and mass are sufficient to manifest gravity and rigidity relations. Smallness is a limitation; excessive smallness reduces the aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, regularity, and comprehensibility of forms and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of the most perfect clearness to perception requires regular figures (straight lines, regular curves) and bodies resulting from them; proportions should be rational and easily comprehensible (simple ratios like 1:2, 2:3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether compositions allow easy surveying and comprehension (symmetry to mark unity, simple numeric proportions). Anti-pattern: obscure or awkward ratios (e.g., 6:7) and irregular interruptions of lines or curves without purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry as marker of unity and intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry is necessary to mark out the work as a whole and to distinguish essential from accidental limitations; it helps the work to announce itself as individual unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry to judge whether a building or composition reads as a coherent unit; asymmetry is acceptable only when it serves a clearly understood structural or perceptual end (e.g., corner columns closer due to increased burden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work in the spirit of nature — avoid aimless caprices
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture (and art) ought to work in the spirit of nature: avoid everything apparently aimless and attain ends by the shortest, most natural path; the naive disclosure of end imparts grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer solutions that openly exhibit their purpose and economize means; penalize designs that 'seek in everything useless roundabout ways' or display caprice disconnected from function (broken entablatures, meaningless volutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate styles by their fundamental thought (antique vs Gothic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antique architecture's fundamental thought is the conflict between rigidity and gravity (objective spirit); Gothic architecture's fundamental thought is the overcoming of gravity by rigidity (subjective spirit) — each expresses a different idea and should be evaluated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing styles, assess consistency with their claimed fundamental thought and judge aesthetic value partly by how well that thought is revealed. Recognize that Gothic's mysterious character often arises from arbitrary or unexplained elements; antique style prizes objective rationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture: prioritize beauty, strength, and fullness
rubrics_metrics.description: In sculpture beauty and grace are the principal things; sculpture demands beauty (not always perfect) and strength and fullness of the figures; thin, emaciated forms can be repulsive in sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sculptural works for fullness and muscular strength appropriate to material; penalize reduction to skin-and-bone where marble demands idealized fullness. Example contrast: a thin Christ may be proper for painting but repulsive in marble sculpture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting: prioritize expression, passion, and character
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting expression, passion, and character predominate; painting may present ugly faces and emaciated figures in virtue of expressive ends and thus may legitimately neglect some claims of ideal beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge paintings more on expressive power and conveyed character than on classical bodily beauty; allow purposeful departure from ideal form when it serves expressive content (e.g., a wasting saint in painting can be appropriate).
